title: Mass vs Weight
keyIdea: Mass is the amount of matter in an object, measured in kilograms (kg) with a balance; it is the same everywhere. Weight is the force of gravity on that mass, measured in newtons (N) with a newtonmeter. Weight = mass × gravitational field strength, W = m × g. On Earth g is about 10 N/kg (9.8), so a 2 kg bag weighs 20 N. On the Moon g is 1.6 N/kg, so the same bag weighs only 3.2 N, but its mass is still 2 kg. To find a mass from a weight, divide: m = W ÷ g.
familyTip: Find a food packet that says its mass, such as 500 g. Ask: what would it weigh in newtons here (about 5 N), and on the Moon? Then ask whether the packet holds any less food on the Moon.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: hang masses on a newtonmeter and plot weight, take a 2 kg bag to the Moon, Mars and Jupiter with a balance, and use W = m × g both ways.

kid: Mass is how much stuff is in something. We measure it in kilograms, kg. A balance finds mass by comparing it with known masses. Your mass is the same on Earth, on the Moon, or in space.
Weight is a force. It is the pull of gravity on your mass. We measure it in newtons, N, with a newtonmeter. A newtonmeter is a spring that stretches more when the pull is bigger.
On Earth, gravity pulls on each kilogram with about 10 N. This is called the gravitational field strength, g. So weight = mass × g. A 2 kg bag weighs 2 × 10 = 20 N.
The Moon pulls less. Its g is 1.6 N/kg, so the 2 kg bag weighs only 3.2 N there. Jupiter pulls more, with g = 25 N/kg, so the bag weighs 50 N. In all three places its mass is 2 kg.
adult: Ages 11 to 12. The KS3 physics programme of study for England (motion and forces) includes non-contact forces: gravity force, weight = mass × gravitational field strength (g); on Earth g = 10 N/kg, different on other planets and stars. NGSS MS-PS2-4 asks pupils to argue from evidence that gravitational interactions are attractive and depend on the masses of the objects. Words to use: mass, kilogram, weight, force, newton, newtonmeter, balance, gravitational field strength.

Mass is a property of the object; weight is a force that depends on where the object is. The lab uses g = 10 N/kg for Earth (9.8 N/kg is more exact), 1.6 N/kg for the Moon, 3.7 N/kg for Mars and 25 N/kg for Jupiter. A spring newtonmeter reads weight, so its reading changes from world to world. A pan balance compares two masses that are both pulled by the same g, so it gives the same result everywhere. Bathroom scales show kilograms, but they measure the push of your weight and are set for Earth's g.

Common mistakes: using kg as the unit of weight, or saying an object weighs 2 kg; thinking mass gets smaller on the Moon; thinking there is no gravity on the Moon or in orbit; adding m and g instead of multiplying; and multiplying by g again when working back from a weight to a mass. In the lab each wrong option is built from one of these slips and its message names it.

practice.prompt: A 2 kg bag hangs on a newtonmeter on Earth (g = 10 N/kg). What does it read?
practice.hint: Weight = mass × g. Give the answer in newtons.
practice.explain: W = 2 kg × 10 N/kg = 20 N. A newtonmeter reads a force, so the answer is in newtons, not kilograms.

practice.prompt: What does a {m} kg object weigh on Earth, where g = 10 N/kg? Give the answer in N.
practice.hint: Multiply the mass in kg by 10 N/kg.

practice.prompt: A newtonmeter on Earth (g = 10 N/kg) reads {=10*m} N. What is the mass in kg?
practice.hint: To go from weight back to mass, divide by g.

practice.prompt: You take a 2 kg bag to the Moon. What is its mass there?
practice.hint: Does the bag lose any matter on the trip?
practice.explain: Mass is the amount of matter, so it stays 2 kg. Its weight drops from 20 N to 2 × 1.6 = 3.2 N.

practice.prompt: On Mars g = 3.7 N/kg. What does a 10 kg box weigh there?
practice.hint: Multiply the mass by g, and use newtons.
practice.explain: W = 10 × 3.7 = 37 N. 13.7 N adds instead of multiplying, and kg is the unit of mass.

pool.hint: Weight is a force. Which instrument is a spring pulled by gravity?
pool.explain: A newtonmeter's spring stretches with the pull of gravity, so it measures weight in newtons. A balance compares masses.

pool.prompt: Why does a pan balance give the same answer on the Moon as on Earth?
choices: Gravity pulls both pans the same way, so it compares masses
There is no gravity on the Moon
The balance is lighter on the Moon
pool.hint: What happens to both sides of the balance when g changes?
pool.explain: Both pans are pulled by the same g, so they still balance when the masses are equal. That is why a balance shows mass.

pool.prompt: What does a {m} kg rock weigh on Jupiter, where g = 25 N/kg? Give the answer in N.
pool.hint: Weight = mass × g. Multiply the mass by 25 N/kg.
pool.explain: W = {m} × 25 = {=m*25} N. On Earth the same rock would weigh {=m*10} N.

pool.prompt: An astronaut weighs 800 N on Earth (g = 10 N/kg). What is her mass?
pool.hint: Go from weight back to mass: divide the weight by g.
pool.explain: m = 800 ÷ 10 = 80 kg. 8,000 comes from multiplying by g again.

pool.prompt: A 70 kg astronaut goes to the Moon (g = 1.6 N/kg). What is her weight there?
pool.hint: Use W = m × g with the Moon's g.
pool.explain: W = 70 × 1.6 = 112 N. Her mass is still 70 kg; 700 N is her weight on Earth.

choices: Weight is a force, measured in newtons
pool.hint: Which one is the pull of gravity?
pool.explain: Weight is the force of gravity on a mass, in newtons. Mass, in kg, stays the same on every planet.

pool.prompt: On Mars (g = 3.7 N/kg) a box weighs {=37*k} N. What is its mass in kg?
Why does the same bag weigh less on the Moon than on Earth?
choices: The Moon's gravitational field is weaker
The bag has less matter on the Moon
There is no air on the Moon
pool.hint: The bag is the same. What is different about the Moon's pull?
pool.explain: The Moon has much less mass than Earth, so its g is only 1.6 N/kg. The bag's matter, and so its mass, does not change.
